title: Auctions
description: Auctions turn competing offers into a decision about who gets something, making the rules of bidding part of the outcome.
opening_html:
A community theatre has one donated painting and many interested buyers. Nobody knows what it will sell for. An auction lets the buyers reveal offers, then uses an announced rule to choose a winner and a price. The theatre can raise money without first guessing the right asking price.

That simple idea contains several different arrangements. In an ascending auction, bidders can respond to one another. In a sealed-bid auction, they submit offers without seeing competing bids. Auction design changes what participants learn and how they bid; the winner need not always pay the number written on their own offer.

sections.title: What the bid measures
sections.html:
The highest bid identifies the person willing and able to pay most under those rules. It does not identify who needs the painting most, or who would give it the best home. Auctions are powerful precisely because they make one criterion decisive; they become misleading when that criterion is mistaken for every kind of value.

For the theatre, several independent bidders make the process more informative. If the only two serious buyers agree to keep their bids low, the ceremony of competition remains while much of its substance disappears. The object, information available to bidders, and opportunities for collusion all belong to the design.

title: Double auctions
description: Double auctions let buyers and sellers make offers at the same time, creating prices through repeated opportunities to trade.
opening_html:
Imagine several workshops selling surplus fabric while local designers look for material. Sellers post quantities and minimum prices; buyers post what they want and what they will pay. When compatible offers meet, a trade can happen. Nobody has to calculate a single price that satisfies everyone before exchange begins.

This is a double auction: offers come from both sides. Unlike an auction organized around one seller's object, it can support repeated trading among many participants. Repeated offers can coordinate information scattered across buyers and sellers, without everyone revealing their full circumstances.

sections.title: A market needs participants
sections.html:
Suppose one workshop lowers its asking price after a week without a sale. A designer who previously waited now buys. Other participants see an opportunity to revise their own offers. Prices emerge through these adjustments rather than through a survey of everyone's private circumstances.

But a list of offers is not automatically a useful market. Fabric grades, collection arrangements, and quantities need to be comparable enough for an apparent match to mean something. With one large buyer and many desperate sellers, the ability to post a bid does not imply equal bargaining power. Thin participation can leave the page full of offers and almost no actual exchange.

title: Barter
description: Barter lets people exchange useful goods or work directly, provided each can offer something the other actually wants.
opening_html:
A photographer needs a bicycle repaired; a repairer needs photographs for a new workshop. They could exchange those services instead of paying one another. Barter makes resources available through a match between needs and capabilities, even when cash is scarce.

The central difficulty is finding that match. The repairer might need photographs, but not this month. The photographer might offer a portrait session when the repairer needs product images. Money normally separates these decisions; a direct exchange of goods or services brings them back together.

sections.title: Agreeing on the exchange
sections.html:
The photographer and repairer still need to settle what counts as completion: which repairs, how many photographs, and whether replacement parts are included. Avoiding a price tag does not make valuation disappear. It moves valuation into a conversation about the actual exchange.

A network can improve the chances of finding partners, but a system that lets someone earn credit from one person and spend it with another has added an accounting mechanism beyond simple direct barter. That distinction matters: the network must then sustain confidence in its credits as well as in its individual members. Here the smaller promise is enough—two parties recognize a mutually useful exchange and make its terms understandable.

title: Mutual credit
description: Mutual credit lets a network exchange before everyone has cash, recording what members have supplied and received in shared accounts.
opening_html:
A printer wants help designing a brochure. The designer needs furniture, and a furniture maker needs printing. Direct barter would require a fortunate match between two people. A mutual-credit network can connect all three: purchases create negative balances and sales create positive balances in a shared ledger.

The credit is useful because other participants accept it. It is not a pile of money someone necessarily deposited beforehand. In the Sardex network, commercial relationships help keep credits circulating; maintaining the ledger is only part of maintaining the exchange.

sections.title: Balances need somewhere to go
sections.html:
Imagine the printer earns a large positive balance but cannot find anything useful to buy. The ledger says the printer has contributed; the network is failing to return practical value. Recruiting complementary businesses and helping members find trading partners therefore becomes real economic work.

Negative balances also require rules. If members can take indefinitely without supplying anything others want, those holding positive balances lose confidence. Limits, admission decisions, and ways of resolving overdue obligations shape whose promises the network accepts.

Mutual credit changes the timing of exchange and who authorizes purchasing power. It does not manufacture materials, skills, or trustworthy partners. Its possibility lies in connecting productive capacity that exists but cannot easily meet through ordinary cash transactions.

title: Time banking
description: Time banking connects practical help across a community, using hours as credits that members can earn from and spend with different people.
opening_html:
You help a neighbor sort old photographs for two hours. Later, another member helps you assemble a bookshelf. A time bank connects the two exchanges: the person who receives your help does not have to repay you personally.

In the usual model, one hour earns one time credit, whatever the service. This is a deliberate social rule. It makes companionship or patient practical help count in the same unit as a skill that might command a higher market price.

sections.title: A ledger with a host
sections.html:
The arithmetic is easy; making exchanges happen takes people. A coordinator may introduce members, help someone describe what they can offer, or notice that a person has earned credits but feels uncomfortable requesting help. Without that work, a directory can fill with generous offers that never meet actual requests.

Imagine a member who needs transport but lives far from everyone else. Having credits does not conjure a driver. Travel expenses, accessibility, and the suitability of particular tasks still need attention. Equal hours express how the community chooses to recognize participation; they do not mean all services are equally available.

Time banking gives receiving a place alongside giving. Someone who usually feels like a recipient can become a contributor, while someone accustomed to helping others has an explicit route to ask for help themselves.

title: Local currencies
description: Local currencies give a participating network its own means of payment, encouraging purchases to remain connected to local businesses.
opening_html:
Imagine a town where residents can spend a local currency at the bookshop, bicycle repairer, and several market stalls. Receiving it gives each business a reason to look for another participating supplier. The payment system makes the local trading network visible and potentially useful.

A currency is more than an attractive note or an app balance. People need to know who accepts it, how it enters circulation, and whether it can be exchanged for ordinary money. BerkShares connects participating businesses in a local payment network.

sections.title: Acceptance is the infrastructure
sections.html:
Suppose the bookshop takes many local payments but pays its major distributor outside town. It may need a reliable conversion route. A repairer purchasing tools locally may find the same currency easier to reuse. Identical balances can therefore have different practical value to different businesses.

The network's reach matters more than the slogan printed on the currency. If it connects businesses that can buy from one another, spending can circulate. If acceptance is patchy, users may treat it as an inconvenient gift voucher.

Keeping a transaction inside a named area also does not establish that new economic activity occurred or that benefits were evenly shared. The specific opportunity is to organize local exchange relationships; evaluating the wider result requires looking at who trades, what becomes possible, and who remains outside the network.

title: Gift economies
description: Gift economies move resources through ongoing relationships, with expectations of generosity, reciprocity, obligation, or status taking the place of immediate prices.
opening_html:
A friend lends you equipment without naming a fee. Months later, you help them move. Nobody has kept an exact account, yet the relationship contains an expectation that care can flow in both directions. Gift exchange makes room for help whose timing and form cannot be settled in advance.

There is no single rule governing every gift economy. Reciprocity can involve open-ended support or a clearer expectation of a return. Treating every unpaid transfer as the same arrangement hides much of what makes it work.

sections.title: The gift can create a debt
sections.html:
Imagine a neighborhood in which people routinely pass children's clothes to families who need them. A recipient may later contribute something entirely different, or never repay the original giver. The useful unit is the continuing network, not a balanced transaction between two individuals.

But gifts can also establish hierarchy. An extravagant favor from a powerful person may be difficult to refuse and harder to repay. What appears free financially can carry social obligations, invitations that must be accepted, or pressure to show loyalty.

Understanding the arrangement means noticing what recipients are understood to owe, including when the answer is deliberately unspecified. That is where a gift becomes a social technology rather than merely an object changing hands.

title: Reciprocal labor exchanges
description: Reciprocal labor exchanges let people assemble help for demanding tasks by committing to help others when their turn comes.
opening_html:
Some jobs need many hands briefly, rather than one extra worker permanently. Imagine several households restoring storm-damaged fences. They work together at one property this weekend and another next weekend, making concentrated labor available without each household hiring a crew.

The exchange is organized around an obligation to reciprocate. In Andean ayni, labor assistance belongs to continuing community relationships. A one-off work party may assemble the same number of hands, but it need not carry an obligation to return the help later.

sections.title: Whose turn is next?
sections.html:
The schedule carries a promise: accepting help today means remaining available later. That promise is easier to sustain when participants expect continuing relationships and can discuss differences in what each household can contribute.

Suppose one resident has limited mobility but can arrange materials and transport. Counting only hours of physical labor would obscure a contribution the group needs. Conversely, leaving every obligation undefined can turn the most reliable volunteers into a permanent workforce for everyone else.

The group has to make reciprocity understandable without pretending circumstances are identical. Seasonal work, illness, weather, and different task sizes complicate a neat rotation. The attraction is still substantial: a small group can repeatedly create a working crew larger than any member could normally assemble alone.

title: Rotating savings groups
description: Rotating savings groups turn regular small contributions into a larger sum for each member in turn, relying on continued commitment after payout.
opening_html:
Ten people each contribute the same amount every month. Each month, one person receives the entire pot. After ten rounds, everyone has received it once. The arrangement converts a sequence of manageable contributions into a useful lump sum without requiring an outside lender.

The timing changes the deal. Someone receiving the first pot gets access early and keeps paying afterward; someone receiving the last pot has effectively saved through the group. The same rotation gives early recipients credit and later recipients a way to save, supported by everyone’s continuing payments.

sections.title: The promise after payment
sections.html:
Imagine members using their turns for school supplies, equipment, or a household expense. They need an agreed way to set the order before those plans depend on it. Rotation, drawing lots, and other ordering methods create different expectations; the mechanism alone does not decide which is fair.

The vulnerable point is easy to see. A person who receives the pot early might stop contributing, leaving later members short. Personal trust, records, admission rules, and ways of responding to missed payments are therefore central rather than administrative extras.

A group also needs contributions that members can sustain. A strict schedule can support saving, but it can become a burden when someone's income is irregular. The pot is created by the members' commitments, so a disruption passes through the whole circle.

title: Credit unions
description: Credit unions place financial services under member ownership, giving users a formal role in governing the institution they depend on.
opening_html:
Your bank's customers and owners can be different groups. In a credit union, membership connects those roles: the people using the institution collectively own it and elect its governing board. That changes who the institution is formally organized to serve.

The member-owned cooperative model does not mean every member makes every lending decision. Staff still handle daily operations, while governance determines broader direction and oversight. Owning a vote and running a financial institution are different responsibilities.

sections.title: Ownership needs attention
sections.html:
Imagine a credit union considering whether to maintain a small branch. Members who rely on face-to-face service may value it even if it is less profitable than another location. Member governance provides a route for that concern to affect the decision, alongside the costs of keeping the institution viable.

A formal vote can nevertheless become remote from ordinary members' lives. If few people participate, a small circle may exercise most practical influence. Financial expertise and understandable reporting are both necessary: members need usable information, and elected representatives need the ability to oversee complex operations.

Ownership also does not remove lending losses or other financial risks. The distinctive social mechanism is that users have an institutional claim on governance and purpose. Whether they can exercise it effectively depends on the institution's rules, capacity, and actual participation.

title: Mutual insurance
description: Mutual insurance combines shared protection with policyholder ownership, connecting the people exposed to losses with the institution managing their coverage.
opening_html:
A household cannot predict exactly when a costly loss will happen. Many households can contribute to a fund that pays covered claims when losses occur. Mutual insurance adds a governance choice to that familiar pooling mechanism: policyholders are members of the insurance organization rather than only its customers.

This creates a connection between protection and collective ownership. Policyholders participate as members of the institution, with rights defined by its particular structure.

sections.title: A promise that must survive claims
sections.html:
Imagine members debating whether to expand a category of coverage. A wider promise may help households facing a neglected risk, but it also changes what the common fund must be able to pay. The decision links solidarity with arithmetic: generosity on paper is of little use if the institution cannot meet claims.

Policyholder ownership does not settle disagreements about prices, eligibility, or what counts as a covered loss. People with different exposures may want different rules, and professional staff still hold information most members lack.

The mutual form creates a way to govern those tensions through an institution owned by the protected group. It does not replace adequate reserves, competent administration, or fair claims handling. Those are the practical work through which a promise of mutual protection becomes dependable.

title: Emergency mutual-aid funds
description: Emergency mutual-aid funds turn contributions from a network into timely help for members facing expenses they cannot manage alone.
opening_html:
A broken wheelchair or an unexpected move can become a crisis because the money is needed now. An emergency mutual-aid fund gathers contributions before or during such moments and distributes help without expecting recipients to repay a loan.

The fund makes solidarity actionable: there is somewhere to ask, a process for deciding, and money available to transfer. The Elswick Solidarity Fund organizes requests around available funds and community review, giving community support a practical route to reach people.

sections.title: Speed and dignity
sections.html:
Imagine a neighborhood fund receiving more requests than it can cover. Demanding elaborate proof might protect scarce resources but delay help and expose private hardship. Relying entirely on personal familiarity can instead favor the people organizers already know.

This is why the request process matters as much as fundraising. A person needs to understand what information is required, who sees it, and how a decision arrives. Organizers need a workable way to handle limited funds without turning every request into a public trial of deservingness.

Regular small contributions can make the fund less dependent on a dramatic appeal. Even then, it remains a bounded resource. Its particular strength is responding to needs that a community can recognize quickly, with a form of assistance that does not add another repayment obligation to an already difficult situation.

title: Crowdfunding
description: Crowdfunding lets many supporters finance a project together, while the promises attached to their contributions determine what relationship they are entering.
opening_html:
A small museum wants to digitize a collection. Hundreds of people care, but none can fund the whole job. A public campaign lets their contributions accumulate around a concrete proposal, making a dispersed audience capable of financing shared work.

The word crowdfunding covers different promises. Donations, rewards, loans, and investments give contributors different expectations. A thank-you postcard is not a repayment obligation as in crowdlending; a promised product is not ownership in the organization.

sections.title: Funding is one milestone
sections.html:
Imagine the museum reaches its target. It now has the money to begin scanning, but still needs permission to publish images, reliable equipment, and staff time. The total raised measures support for the campaign. It does not establish that the promised work has been completed.

Campaign design also selects for some kinds of work. A vivid restoration project may attract attention more easily than maintaining the archive afterward. Preparing updates, answering supporters, and delivering rewards can become substantial work of their own.

Crowdfunding is especially interesting when it gathers people who already value something but have no established organization through which to support it. The campaign briefly gives that scattered public a shared object, a visible commitment, and a way to act together.

title: Crowdlending
description: Crowdlending gathers money from multiple lenders for borrowers, turning many individual commitments into financing with expected repayment.
opening_html:
A project may have supporters willing to lend rather than donate. Crowdlending organizes those offers through a platform, connecting borrowers with multiple people whose contributions together finance a loan. Repayment is central to the relationship: the money is intended to come back under agreed terms.

The platform does more than display a fundraising page. It helps arrange and administer the lending relationship, which distinguishes loan-based from donation-based crowdfunding.

sections.title: Many lenders, one obligation
sections.html:
Imagine a small enterprise borrowing to purchase equipment. The enterprise still needs enough income to repay, regardless of how enthusiastic its supporters were. Splitting the financing among many lenders changes where the money comes from; it does not make the borrower's underlying business work.

Lenders also depend on administration: records of repayments, handling missed payments, and a way to understand outstanding balances. If a platform becomes unavailable, the practical organization of those obligations matters as much as the original connection it made.

The social possibility is broader participation in financing. The corresponding difficulty is that a familiar interface and a compelling story can make a loan feel like a simple expression of support. Keeping the repayment promise visible distinguishes crowdlending from the very different act of giving money to a cause.

title: Subscriptions
description: Recurring commitments let many people sustain continuing work, giving its producers a basis for planning beyond the next sale.
opening_html:
A neighborhood magazine wants to investigate why local rents are rising. The reporting may take months, while each issue brings an uncertain number of sales. If enough readers subscribe, their commitments can help pay for the work before the finished story attracts attention. Many small payments become support for something no individual reader would finance alone.

Subscriptions are one way to organize recurring funding. Readers commit to paying for continuing access or delivery; the publisher takes on an obligation to keep producing it. Recurring payments give the publisher a basis for estimating future income. How far ahead it can plan depends on how many people stay, when they pay, and what it has promised them.

sections.title: Enough confidence to keep working
sections.html:
An annual payment in advance can help cover work now. A monthly subscription that can be cancelled at any time offers less certainty, though it may be easier for readers to afford. Neither removes the publisher’s need to earn continued support. If subscriptions fall away, a long investigation may become difficult to finish.

Spreading support across many readers can reduce dependence on a single patron. It also creates a different pressure: work that attracts or retains paying readers becomes easier to fund than work valued by people who cannot subscribe. Who pays helps shape what gets produced.

sections.title: What are people committing to?
sections.html:
A subscriber can remain a customer. Membership dues attach payment to belonging to an association, with whatever rights and responsibilities that association provides. A subscription by itself gives readers no say in who edits the magazine.

Commitments can go further. In some forms of community-supported agriculture, households pay ahead for a share of a farm’s season and accept variation in the harvest. That shares production risk more explicitly than a promise to deliver the same box of vegetables every week. The agreement determines which relationship people are entering.

Continuing payment also needs continuing consent. A reader who has stopped reading may keep paying through inattention or a difficult cancellation process. Revenue sustained that way gives a misleading picture of support. Clear promises, renewal terms, and ways to leave help make recurring funding a relationship people choose to maintain.

title: Membership dues
description: Membership dues finance a continuing association by making contributions part of belonging, rather than asking for a separate donation every time.
opening_html:
A rowing club needs storage, repairs, and a place to meet throughout the year. Individual events may earn money, but the club exists between events too. Membership dues let people jointly maintain that continuing institution.

The payment belongs to a relationship of membership. In clubs such as Rotary clubs, belonging connects regular obligations with shared activities. The exact rights attached to membership vary; paying dues does not inherently mean buying a service package or receiving an equal vote.

sections.title: The price of belonging
sections.html:
Imagine the rowing club charging one flat annual fee. Collection is simple, yet a fee that feels minor to one member may exclude another. Reduced rates, installments, or sponsored memberships can change who is able to remain involved, while also changing how the club covers its costs.

Dues make maintenance visible. Members are contributing to the boats being usable next season, not only to the outing they attend today. That can support continuity when particular activities have uneven attendance.

The relationship becomes strained if members cannot understand what their money sustains or how decisions are made. A healthy dues system therefore has an organizational counterpart: a recognizable membership, responsibilities people can explain, and an institution whose continued existence members consider worth supporting.

title: Patronage
description: Patronage gives a person or institution sustained support from a particular backer, opening possibilities while making the relationship itself a source of influence.
opening_html:
A researcher wants to pursue an idea that does not fit an existing grant competition. A patron might support the work because they trust the researcher, care about the question, or want the resulting achievement associated with their name. That personal judgment can finance work before a larger institution knows how to evaluate it.

Patronage can support a specific commission or a longer relationship. In artistic commissions, patrons could influence which subjects were depicted and which artists received work.

sections.title: Freedom with a relationship attached
sections.html:
Imagine a supporter funding a local oral-history project for several years. Stable backing could let interviewers earn trust and follow leads that a short deadline would cut off. The same dependence becomes difficult if the supporter dislikes an interview about their own family or business.

The influence need not take the form of an explicit instruction. A creator who knows the next payment depends on one person's approval may anticipate that person's preferences. A generous relationship can therefore create both unusual freedom and a narrow source of vulnerability.

Patronage differs from a broad subscriber base because a particular relationship carries much of the support. Its distinctive potential is patient, discretionary backing. Its central tension is who gets to direct the work when the creator's judgment and the patron's wishes diverge.

title: Grants
description: Grants let institutions fund proposed work without buying a normal commercial product, using applications and assessment to choose what receives support.
opening_html:
A community archive wants to record elders' memories before they disappear. The people who benefit may never be able to pay the full cost. A grant can supply resources because a funder values the work, rather than because the project can sell enough tickets or subscriptions.

To make that decision, the funder usually needs a proposal: what will happen, who will do it, what it will cost, and why it matters. Programs such as Grants for Arts Projects turn those judgments into an application and review process.

sections.title: What can fit in an application
sections.html:
The application makes a project legible to strangers. It can also reshape the project. Imagine the archive adding public events because those are easy to describe as outcomes, even though cataloguing existing recordings is its most urgent need.

Restricted funding can pay for a visible activity while leaving the organization struggling with rent, administration, or maintenance. Preparing applications also takes time; groups with experienced grant writers can express their work in the funder's preferred language more easily than equally capable newcomers.

Grants create room for work that lacks a straightforward paying customer. Their influence reaches beyond the projects selected: eligibility rules, deadlines, and reporting requirements help determine which ambitions organizations learn to propose in the first place.

title: Prize competitions
description: Prize competitions invite people to solve a defined challenge, rewarding selected results while leaving competitors to choose their own approaches.
opening_html:
An organizer wants a new way to inspect damaged bridges but does not know which technical approach will work. A prize competition can name the desired result, define a test, and invite different teams to try. It buys an incentive to attempt a problem rather than a guaranteed amount of labor from one contractor.

That freedom is paired with uncertainty for entrants. Inducement prize competitions generally award selected qualifying results; other teams may spend substantial resources and receive no prize.

sections.title: The target is not the whole purpose
sections.html:
Suppose a team wins the bridge challenge with a convincing demonstration. The achievement still leaves questions about routine use: training inspectors, repairing the equipment, and fitting it into existing inspection systems. A judged success, an adopted product, and a durable industry are different outcomes.

The target can also narrow effort. Teams will understandably optimize for what the test rewards. If the test overlooks maintenance costs or difficult conditions, the winner may excel at the competition without solving the larger problem well.

Prize design therefore reaches into financing, measurement, and ownership. A challenge that requires expensive development may mainly attract teams already able to raise capital. A smaller, well-defined challenge can invite contributors the organizer would never have thought to hire. The competition changes who gets to attempt a solution, but its rules decide what counts as success.

A prize can offer an inventor a return without relying on patent exclusivity, but only if the reward and access terms are designed that way. It does not automatically pay for unsuccessful attempts or require the winning invention to be openly usable.

title: Bounties
description: Bounties attach a reward to an accepted result, allowing people outside a regular team to decide whether a specific contribution is worth attempting.
opening_html:
A volunteer-run map is missing the locations of accessible entrances to public buildings. Organizers could offer a bounty for each verified entry that meets their requirements. Instead of recruiting someone for an ongoing role, they publish a result they are willing to reward.

The crucial words are “verified” and “meets their requirements.” Vulnerability bounty programs define which findings qualify, how to report them, and how they will be assessed. A mapping bounty needs similarly clear acceptance conditions.

sections.title: A reward needs an acceptance rule
sections.html:
In the map project, two people might submit the same entrance. One might record coordinates without a usable photograph. A building might be accessible only at certain times. Each ambiguity becomes a decision about whether the promised reward is owed.

Clear acceptance rules make the offer understandable before contributors invest effort. They also reveal work that the bounty leaves out: checking submissions, resolving duplicates, correcting errors, and maintaining the information later.

Unlike a salary, the bounty does not pay simply for time spent trying. That can attract unexpected contributors with useful local knowledge, but it transfers uncertainty to them. A program with unreliable judging can exhaust goodwill quickly, even when its public list of rewards looks generous.

title: Participatory budgeting
description: Participatory budgeting gives people a direct role in choosing how part of a shared budget is spent, turning preferences into funded projects.
opening_html:
Residents can ask for safer crossings year after year without knowing whether their request will survive a budgeting process. Participatory budgeting gives them a defined share of money and a route to decide what it should fund. The decision becomes more concrete than a consultation about general priorities.

A typical process moves from ideas to developed proposals, voting, and implementation. Before a proposal reaches the ballot, community members and staff develop it into something feasible to fund.

sections.title: Between the idea and the ballot
sections.html:
Imagine residents choosing among shade trees, accessible paths, and new lighting. Each idea needs a realistic cost and a check that the money can actually pay for it. Staff and community delegates help turn ambitions into proposals; their judgments therefore shape the choices voters eventually see.

The size and restrictions of the budget also matter. Residents might control a small improvement fund while the largest spending decisions remain elsewhere. Presenting that limited authority accurately is part of making participation credible.

After the vote, someone must procure, build, and maintain the winning projects. If residents can choose but cannot learn why delivery stalls, a promising transfer of authority becomes frustrating. The distinctive achievement is connecting public deliberation with an actual spending decision and the administrative work needed to carry it out.

title: Quadratic funding
description: Quadratic funding uses the breadth of small contributions to allocate matching support, giving widespread backing more influence than donation totals alone.
opening_html:
Two projects each collect the same amount. One receives it from a single wealthy supporter; the other receives many small contributions. Ordinary fundraising treats the totals as equal. Quadratic funding is designed to notice the difference and direct more matching support toward broader participation.

Its basic calculation squares the sum of the square roots of individual contributions. An outside subsidy supplies the matching funds, so contributors’ payments can attract additional resources.

sections.title: Counting people changes the game
sections.html:
Imagine a community funding public workshops. A beginner-friendly project backed by many small donors could receive more matching money than a specialist project with one large donation. That is a choice about what the fund wants to reward, not proof that the broader project is better in every respect.

Once the number of contributors matters, identity matters too. One person pretending to be many people can distort the result. Groups can also coordinate donations to capture matching funds. Verification and rules against collusion become part of the mechanism rather than optional platform features.

A finite matching pool introduces another constraint: supporting one project affects what remains for others. The amount available, the reliability of identities, and coordination among donors can all change how closely the allocation reflects independent support.

title: Matching grants
description: Matching grants make outside funding conditional on additional contributions, encouraging supporters to assemble resources around a common project.
opening_html:
A neighborhood association has some support for restoring a small public garden, but not enough to begin. A matching grant can promise additional funding if the association raises an eligible contribution of its own. Each new commitment helps unlock another source of money.

The required match need not always be cash. Programs define what counts, and some accept specified in-kind contributions. Challenge America, for example, specifies which cash and in-kind contributions can satisfy its match.

sections.title: The match selects for capacity
sections.html:
Imagine two equally useful garden proposals. One neighborhood has several wealthy supporters; the other has residents willing to contribute labor but little spare money. A cash-only matching requirement would make the first proposal easier to finance, even if the second community's need were greater.

For the funder, a match can indicate commitment and spread costs. For organizers, it creates another fundraising task and sometimes a deadline that shapes the project. Pledges also need to become usable resources at the right moment: a promise arriving after contractors must be paid may not solve the immediate problem.

The mechanism brings multiple backers into one project. Its practical effect depends on what contributions are recognized and who already has the networks, reserves, and time needed to assemble them.

title: Endowments
description: Endowments turn accumulated assets into continuing institutional support, connecting present spending with obligations to people who will come later.
opening_html:
A library receives a large gift. It could spend the money immediately on a new building, or preserve an invested fund whose distributions help operate the library over many years. An endowment organizes the second possibility: support that continues beyond one fundraising campaign.

The fund connects generations of donors, trustees, and beneficiaries. At Harvard, endowment assets support distributions over time, and many gifts are restricted to particular purposes. A large total therefore differs from money freely available to spend today.

sections.title: Wealth is not a free spending account
sections.html:
Imagine a library whose endowment supports rare-book conservation while its public reading room needs repairs. The institution can look wealthy in aggregate yet lack permission to use a particular fund for the urgent expense. Donor restrictions make past choices persist inside present budgets.

Spending decisions also divide resources across time. Drawing more now may improve services for current readers while reducing future support; preserving too much may leave useful work undone today. Investment outcomes add uncertainty to both sides of that decision.

An endowment gives an institution some independence from annual appeals or changing funders. It also creates a permanent governance task: translating the purpose of accumulated wealth into a sustainable flow of activity. A board of trustees can be entrusted with that oversight. The fund is meaningful because of the work it supports, not simply because its balance survives.

title: Pooled procurement
description: Pooled procurement joins separate organizations’ purchasing needs into a coordinated order, making their combined demand easier to negotiate and fulfill.
opening_html:
Several small organizations need the same equipment but place separate orders, repeat the same checks, and negotiate from a weak position. Pooled procurement brings those requirements together. A shared purchasing arrangement can make demand more predictable for suppliers and let buyers combine specialist procurement work.

The Global Fund’s pooled purchasing coordinates financing, specifications, approvals, and delivery arrangements. Adding quantities is only the beginning. Buying clubs organize a related form of joint purchasing among members.

sections.title: One order, many destinations
sections.html:
Imagine a network of community workshops buying replacement safety equipment. Combining demand might help secure a useful price, but only if the equipment actually fits each workshop's needs. One group's required specification cannot simply disappear into a convenient common order.

The network also needs to know who pays when, where goods arrive, and what happens if a participant changes its request. A large order delivered to the wrong place is not a purchasing success for the organization waiting to use it.

Pooling can concentrate dependence as well as bargaining power. Selecting one supplier may simplify administration while leaving everyone exposed to the same delay. The mechanism works through coordinated commitments: buyers surrender some freedom to order independently in exchange for the possibilities created by acting as a larger customer.

title: Buying clubs
description: Buying clubs let people or small enterprises combine purchases while remaining independent, sharing the work and advantages of ordering together.
opening_html:
A group of independent makers all need packaging, but each buys too little to obtain a useful bulk price. A buying club lets them combine orders without merging their businesses. Members remain responsible for their own work while cooperating on one recurring need.

Farmers can organize purchases through buying clubs while continuing to run their own farms. The club can be much narrower than a full cooperative business.

sections.title: The hidden job is distribution
sections.html:
Imagine the makers placing one large order for boxes. Someone must collect quantities, receive payments, store the shipment, and divide it correctly. If that person quietly contributes several unpaid evenings each month, the apparent saving partly comes from their labor.

Minimum order sizes can also leave members purchasing more than they need. A cheap unit price is less attractive when excess stock fills a small workspace. Different members may prefer different suppliers or have incompatible cash-flow schedules.

A workable buying club makes those practical commitments visible. It can remain lightweight because its common purpose is bounded: buy these things together, under an agreed arrangement. That small piece of coordination can give independent participants access to purchasing conditions otherwise available mainly to larger organizations.

A producer cooperative can go further by giving producers shared ownership of processing or marketing facilities. A buying club need only organize the purchases its members have agreed to make together.

title: Tool libraries
description: Tool libraries make useful equipment available through borrowing, turning occasional needs into a shared inventory instead of repeated individual purchases.
opening_html:
You may need a carpet cleaner once a year and a drill for twenty minutes. Owning each item means paying for long periods when it does nothing. A tool library makes temporary access available from a common stock, so many households can use equipment that none needs continuously.

The shelves are only part of the institution. Seattle REconomy's lending arrangements include borrowing periods, returns, renewals, and training requirements. These routines turn donated or purchased objects into dependable access.

sections.title: The return matters as much as the loan
sections.html:
Imagine borrowing a sander for a weekend project. The next borrower has planned their own weekend around receiving it on Monday. Returning it late transfers a problem to someone you may never meet; returning it damaged creates work for volunteers before another loan is possible.

Maintenance, spare parts, storage, and help choosing the right tool are shared costs even when borrowing is inexpensive. A large catalogue can be misleading if popular items are broken or always unavailable.

The library changes the unit of provision from “a tool for every household” to “a usable tool when someone needs one.” That can expand what people are able to repair or build, provided the less glamorous work of keeping the collection functional receives resources too.

title: Resource booking systems
description: Resource booking systems give people a predictable turn with shared equipment or space, translating competing plans into reserved periods of access.
opening_html:
Three groups want the same rehearsal room on Friday evening. A booking system turns those overlapping intentions into an explicit schedule. Each group can plan around an allocation visible to the others instead of negotiating from scratch at the door.

A reservation needs more than a name on a calendar. At Middle Tennessee State University, flight-simulator reservations combine time slots with eligibility and arrival rules. Access, duration, and the ability to cancel all affect whether the schedule corresponds to actual use.

sections.title: A reserved room can still be empty
sections.html:
Imagine one group reserving every Friday just in case, then using the room twice. The calendar looks full while the building stands empty. Booking limits or timely release of unused slots can address that mismatch, but they require someone to administer the rules.

First-come booking also favors people able to plan early and check the system frequently. A group formed yesterday may have a compelling need yet find months of slots already occupied. Priority rules and advance-booking windows determine how the system treats that situation.

The technology is valuable because it makes future access credible. Its fairness depends on the allocation rule underneath the interface, and its reliability depends on people honoring reservations or making unused time available again.

title: Queues
description: Queues organize access through an agreed waiting order, replacing repeated contests for attention with a visible rule for whose turn comes next.
opening_html:
At a crowded repair desk, everyone wants the next available technician. A queue lets people stop continually competing for attention. Once their place is recognized, they can expect service after those ahead of them.

The line can be physical or recorded through numbered tickets. Wimbledon uses numbered, nontransferable queue cards to make waiting order explicit. The rule becomes something staff and participants can both refer to.

sections.title: Waiting is a kind of price
sections.html:
Imagine two people who each need a fifteen-minute repair. One has a free afternoon; the other must return to a shift in half an hour. Equal places in a first-come queue do not impose equal burdens. Waiting uses time, mobility, and flexibility that people possess in different amounts.

A ticket system may let someone sit down or leave briefly, changing the practical cost without changing their order. Priority access for urgent needs changes the ordering principle itself. Both can be reasonable, but people need to understand which promise the queue makes.

A queue's quiet achievement is preventing every service encounter from becoming a negotiation. Its limit is that arriving first answers one allocation question, not every question about need, fairness, or efficient use of the resource.

title: Allocation lotteries
description: Allocation lotteries use chance to choose among eligible applicants, avoiding fine-grained rankings when there is no agreed way to distinguish equally valid claims.
opening_html:
A community arts course has twenty places and fifty applicants who meet its requirements. Organizers could invent a ranking of enthusiasm, reward the fastest applications, or draw names. A lottery makes selection random within the pool they have chosen to admit.

When school admissions use random allocation, the draw operates within an eligible group of applicants. The random step does not decide who belongs in the pool; that decision has already been made.

The same random mechanism can serve a different purpose in sortition, which selects people for responsibilities rather than allocating a scarce benefit. Deciding what the draw distributes is as important as deciding how to conduct it.

sections.title: Equal chances have a boundary
sections.html:
Imagine the arts course requiring applications through a short online form. Even a perfectly conducted draw excludes people who never heard about it, could not use the form, or misunderstood the deadline. Randomness removes certain judgments from selection without removing the effects of the surrounding process.

The draw also needs understandable administration. A list of eligible applicants, a stated procedure, and a way to handle withdrawals make the result easier to trust. Otherwise, “chosen at random” can become a claim nobody can inspect.

A lottery can be a modest admission that the organizer lacks a defensible reason to rank one qualifying person above another. It gives each a chance while leaving the deeper scarcity untouched: thirty people still need another opportunity.

title: Needs-based allocation
description: Needs-based allocation directs scarce resources toward the people facing the most urgent or serious shortfalls, rather than rewarding arrival time or purchasing power.
opening_html:
A heatwave leaves several buildings without reliable cooling. Distributing fans equally among everyone who asks may overlook residents whose circumstances make heat especially difficult to escape. Needs-based allocation tries to distinguish those situations before dividing the available help.

The principle is explicit in humanitarian impartiality: assistance follows assessed need rather than political affiliation or another unrelated preference. Applying it requires more than declaring concern; someone must decide which information establishes urgency.

sections.title: Need must become visible
sections.html:
During the distribution, people who can explain their circumstances confidently may be easiest to assess. Someone isolated, undocumented in the organizers' records, or reluctant to disclose private information may be harder to see. Confidentiality agreements can define how disclosed information may be used. The assessment process can therefore change whose needs count in practice.

Different shortfalls may also resist a single ranking. One household lacks transport, another cannot leave an upper-floor room, and a third needs help reaching an existing cooling space. Equal quantities of the same item might not provide equal relief.

Needs-based allocation is a commitment to attend to those differences. It can redirect resources away from the loudest or wealthiest claimants, but it also places responsibility on assessors to make judgments that are explainable, revisable, and accessible to the people whose circumstances they may have misunderstood.

title: Rationing
description: Rationing limits how much people may obtain from a scarce supply, spreading access through explicit allowances rather than leaving distribution entirely to price.
opening_html:
When a needed resource is scarce, unrestricted purchasing can let a few buyers take most of it. Rationing introduces an allowance: a maximum quantity a person or household may obtain during a period. The intention is to preserve access for others who also depend on the supply.

Britain’s wartime food system used ration books and coupons to administer allowances. An allowance organizes claims on supply; it does not by itself produce the goods.

sections.title: Equal allowances, different lives
sections.html:
Imagine a shared water tank during a temporary disruption. A per-household limit is simple, but households contain different numbers of people. A per-person limit addresses that difference while raising new questions about visitors, records, and uses that require extra water.

People also need a practical route to claim their allowance. A formal entitlement is little help if collection happens only when someone cannot leave work. Distribution arrangements belong to rationing just as much as the number printed on a card.

The system can be undermined by hidden purchases, hoarding, or preferential treatment. Its value lies in making scarcity a collective allocation problem, rather than pretending everyone can obtain enough by trying harder. Its legitimacy depends on whether the limits and exceptions remain understandable to those living under them.

title: Tradable quotas
description: Tradable quotas combine a collective limit with transferable shares, letting participants exchange permissions while the overall allowance remains bounded.
opening_html:
A regulator can limit an activity by setting a total allowance and dividing it into quotas. Making those quotas transferable adds a second mechanism: eligible holders can buy or sell permission instead of every allocation remaining fixed.

In fisheries, some catch-share arrangements permit transfers and others do not. The shared feature is a bounded entitlement, while tradability changes how that entitlement can move between participants.

sections.title: The first allocation keeps mattering
sections.html:
Imagine a fishery dividing an allowed catch among existing operators. Those initial rights could become valuable assets. A newcomer may need to acquire a quota before participating, while an established holder may benefit even after reducing their own activity.

Transfers can let participants adjust to changing circumstances, but they can also concentrate control. The rule for who may hold a quota, and how much, becomes part of the institution's distribution of power.

Most importantly, the trading system does not establish whether the overall limit is appropriate or whether actual activity stays inside it. That requires credible measurement and enforcement. A well-functioning exchange of permissions can coexist with a poorly chosen cap. The market coordinates use of the allowance; the surrounding governance remains responsible for defining and protecting the limit.

title: Commons governance
description: Commons governance lets people organize continuing use and care of a shared resource through rules they can understand, maintain, and revise together.
opening_html:
A shared woodland can supply fuel, support wildlife, and remain useful for future generations. Each user may benefit from taking more today, while everyone depends on restraint and maintenance over time. Commons governance addresses that tension through an institution around the resource.

It is not simply permission for anyone to take anything. Communities combine several governing arrangements: access rules, monitoring, participation, consequences, and ways to resolve disputes. The arrangements vary with the resource and the people involved.

sections.title: The common resource has an institution
sections.html:
Imagine woodland users agreeing on collection areas and seasonal limits, while contributing labor to maintain paths. A storm changes the available supply. They now need a way to revise the rules, recognize who has done maintenance, and settle a dispute about an apparent violation.

That work links material knowledge with social relationships. Someone must notice what is happening to the woodland, and people must have reasons to accept the resulting decisions. A rule imported from another place may fit neither the ecology nor local livelihoods.

sections.title: Who may use it, and who may change the rules?
sections.html:
The woodland agreement needs to identify both the resource and the people with rights to use it. Does it include the meadow? May nearby residents gather fallen branches, or only members who maintain the paths? Boundaries need not be fences or identical rights for everyone, but incompatible understandings can turn ordinary use into an apparent violation.

Users also need a recognized way to revise rules as conditions change. A suggestion box can reveal a problem while leaving every decision elsewhere; participation in rulemaking gives users some authority over the response. Their knowledge of seasonal supply and maintenance can then shape the agreement. Meetings dominated by people with spare time may still exclude those most dependent on the resource.

A newly organized group cannot settle every claim simply by drawing a boundary. People who have gathered wood for years may have interests its membership list misses. Establishing access rules means addressing those histories as well as making future responsibilities clear.

sections.title: Notice problems without making every mistake a rupture
sections.html:
Rules need information about both the woodland and its use. Accountable monitors can record damaged paths, changing supplies, and apparent breaches of collection limits. Observation does not automatically determine a penalty: a person needs a way to correct an inaccurate record or explain an unusual circumstance. Selectively recording newcomers’ mistakes while overlooking influential members makes monitoring an instrument of favoritism.

Graduated sanctions distinguish an accidental first breach from repeated disregard of the agreement. A conversation may resolve one problem; temporary restrictions may be needed for another. The purpose is to defend the shared terms while leaving room for correction. Serious harm need not pass through a ritual sequence of minor warnings, and well-connected people should not receive unlimited first chances.

These parts depend on one another. Monitoring a rule users cannot influence can feel like outside control; participation without reliable information can produce decisions detached from the resource. Ostrom’s account of commons institutions connects boundaries, participation, monitoring, and graduated responses with wider arrangements for resolving conflicts and governing across scales. They are design considerations to adapt, not a checklist that guarantees success.

A tool library faces a smaller-scale version of these questions: who may borrow, who maintains the equipment, and what happens after a damaged or overdue return. Resources extending across several communities may instead need several connected decision centers, with local decisions nested in wider arrangements.

The striking possibility is that users can be organizers of a resource's survival, not only competitors for its contents. Yet community is not automatically harmonious: differences in influence, dependence, and access remain inside it. Commons governance is a family of ways to handle those relationships, not a promise that sharing alone solves them.

title: Community land trusts
description: Community land trusts hold land for lasting community benefit, making stewardship persist beyond the preferences of an individual owner or resident.
opening_html:
A neighborhood raises money to make housing affordable. If the homes later sell at unrestricted market prices, the next generation may face the same problem again. A community land trust tries to make the benefit endure by placing land and assets under continuing community stewardship.

Community land trusts can support housing, workspaces, gardens, or other local facilities. They are a way to organize ownership and purpose over time, rather than one universal legal structure.

sections.title: Keeping the next resident in view
sections.html:
In some homeownership models, the trust retains land while residents own homes under agreements that limit resale prices. Those resale formulas connect the present resident's interest in building equity with future residents' need for affordability.

Imagine a trust preserving a small workshop building in an area becoming expensive. Current users may want low rents; future users also need a roof that remains sound. Stewardship has to finance maintenance while keeping the asset available for its intended community.

The trust can protect a purpose from repeated private resale decisions, but it still needs capable governance and resources. “Community” also needs a practical meaning: who may join, who selects leaders, and whose interests are represented when current occupants and the wider neighborhood disagree.

title: Worker cooperatives
description: Worker cooperatives put enterprise ownership and democratic control in the hands of worker-members, changing who has authority over the business they sustain.
opening_html:
A group of translators could sell their labor to an agency owned by someone else, or own an agency together. In a worker cooperative, worker-members have an institutional role in deciding what the business is for and how its results are shared.

The worker cooperative model combines ownership with democratic governance, commonly through one worker-member, one vote. Daily management can still be delegated. Collective ownership does not require every invoice or scheduling decision to become an all-member meeting.

sections.title: Being workers and owners
sections.html:
Imagine the translation cooperative considering a large contract with an unrealistic deadline. Members have to weigh income against workload and reputation. They are no longer only negotiating with an employer about the terms; they share responsibility for the enterprise's decision.

That creates demanding double roles. Members need time and information to govern while also doing their paid work. New workers may face a period before membership, so the distinction between members and employees affects whose voice counts.

Democratic ownership also cannot remove market pressures or business failure. Its distinctive change is constitutional: the people doing the work have a recognized claim on control and financial participation. Whether that becomes meaningful influence depends on understandable accounts, credible elections, and management arrangements that remain answerable to the members.

title: Consumer cooperatives
description: Consumer cooperatives let users collectively own a provider, giving the people buying its goods or services a route to shape its priorities.
opening_html:
A town loses its only general store. Residents could wait for another investor or organize a business they own as customers. A consumer cooperative turns their shared need into a continuing enterprise, with membership connecting use and governance.

Consumer cooperatives operate in many fields, from retail to utilities. Their defining feature is who the members are: the people using the service. That differs from a worker cooperative, whose members participate primarily as workers.

sections.title: Customers become a constituency
sections.html:
Imagine the town's store debating whether to stock an essential item with a low margin. Members can consider its value to the community alongside the need to pay staff and keep the shop open. Consumer ownership gives that judgment a formal place in the business.

It does not automatically give employees the same voice. The interests of customers seeking low prices can conflict with staff seeking better pay or manageable schedules. A consumer cooperative still has to decide how workers are represented and treated.

Participation can also thin out as the enterprise grows. Many members may value the service but leave governance to a small active group. The model creates a constituency with ownership rights; maintaining a living connection between those rights and actual decisions is continuing organizational work.

title: Producer cooperatives
description: Producer cooperatives let independent producers share facilities, services, or market access, making larger-scale coordination possible without merging their entire livelihoods.
opening_html:
Several small orchards can each grow excellent fruit yet struggle to reach buyers, afford storage, or operate packing equipment. A producer cooperative lets them own those shared functions together while keeping their individual farms.

Producer cooperatives can organize processing, marketing, and access to inputs. The members cooperate where scale helps, rather than necessarily pooling all land, equipment, or daily work.

sections.title: One shared business, many independent ones
sections.html:
Imagine the orchards operating a common packing facility. It gives a buyer one place to obtain a reliable shipment, but members must now agree on quality standards, delivery schedules, and how costs are divided. A shared label makes one producer's poor batch a problem for others too.

Large and small producers may value the facility differently. A member supplying most of the volume may expect influence proportional to that contribution, while smaller members may fear being reduced to minor suppliers of their own cooperative. Voting and payment rules decide how those interests meet.

The cooperative adds an institution between isolated producers and a fully integrated company. It can make independent production more viable, but the common services need professional competence and credible commitments from members. Owning a warehouse together helps only when it reliably turns separate output into something buyers can use.

Where the shared need is only buying inputs, a buying club may suffice. Joint ownership of a continuing enterprise adds responsibilities for governing assets and services beyond placing a common order.

title: Housing cooperatives
description: Housing cooperatives connect the right to live somewhere with membership in a collectively governed housing organization, making residents participants in its upkeep and direction.
opening_html:
A leaking roof is normally a landlord's responsibility or an individual owner's problem. In a housing cooperative, residents participate through an organization that owns or controls the housing. Their homes are connected by shared financial and governing responsibilities.

In one common arrangement, members hold shares linked to a right of occupancy rather than separately owning each apartment outright. Other cooperative housing models use different membership and equity arrangements, so the label alone does not establish resale rights or affordability.

sections.title: A home and a shared obligation
sections.html:
Imagine residents deciding whether to postpone a roof replacement to keep monthly charges low. Those on tight budgets may need immediate relief; everyone depends on preventing greater damage later. Cooperative governance brings the disagreement inside an institution residents can influence.

The work does not disappear because there is no outside landlord. Someone must arrange repairs, understand finances, handle arrears, and make decisions about incoming members. Volunteers can become overburdened, while professional management still needs oversight.

Housing cooperatives also differ from communal living. Cohousing, for example, organizes shared spaces and social life; cooperative housing concerns the institution through which residents govern their housing. People can occupy private homes without sharing meals or social lives extensively. The shared element is the housing institution: a way to govern the costs and conditions of residence together. Residents gain a role in those decisions, along with the continuing work of keeping the housing usable and financially sound.

title: Multistakeholder cooperatives
description: Multistakeholder cooperatives give different groups a formal place in governing one enterprise, bringing competing but connected interests into the same institution.
opening_html:
A local food business affects growers, workers, and customers in different ways. Growers want dependable prices, workers need decent conditions, and customers want affordable goods. A multistakeholder cooperative can make more than one of these groups a class of members.

The arrangement goes beyond asking outsiders for feedback. Multiple member groups share control, although their voting rights and representation need an explicit design. Including everyone in the name does not tell you how decisions are made.

sections.title: The disagreement moves inside
sections.html:
Imagine the food cooperative considering longer opening hours. Customers would gain convenience, staff would face different shifts, and suppliers might receive more orders. Representatives can negotiate those effects within a shared business instead of treating them solely as conflicts between separate parties.

But one group may have many more members, money, or time than another. A simple headcount vote could make the smaller constituency irrelevant; reserved seats can protect its voice while introducing different questions about legitimacy and deadlock.

The purpose is not to pretend interests coincide. It is to create durable relationships through which people who depend on the same enterprise can govern their differences. That takes more negotiation than a cooperative serving only consumer members, and the additional complexity needs to earn its place by improving decisions that matter.

title: Employee ownership
description: Employee ownership gives workers a stake in the enterprise employing them, while separate rules determine whether that stake also carries governing power.
opening_html:
A business owner plans to retire. Selling to an outside buyer is one possibility; transferring an ownership stake to employees is another. Employee ownership can connect workers' financial interests with the enterprise they have helped build.

The phrase covers different arrangements. An employee stock ownership plan is one particular vehicle, not a synonym for a worker cooperative. Having an ownership interest and having an equal vote over management are distinct things.

sections.title: A stake is not the whole constitution
sections.html:
Imagine employees receiving shares while an existing board continues to direct the company. Workers may participate in financial gains without gaining much influence over schedules or strategy. Another arrangement might give them meaningful representation. Both can involve employee ownership, but the experience of working there can differ substantially.

Ownership also ties part of a person's financial position to the organization providing their income. If the company struggles, employment and the value of the stake may both suffer. The institutional design determines when interests can be sold or transferred and who represents them.

The important change is that workers are included among the owners. Understanding its practical significance requires following the associated rights: who votes, who receives proceeds, how people enter and leave, and what information owners can obtain about the business.

title: Steward ownership
description: Steward ownership organizes company control around its continuing purpose, restricting the ability to treat governing rights simply as an asset for sale.
opening_html:
A founder wants a useful company to continue after their departure without its purpose being traded away to the highest bidder. Steward ownership addresses that ambition by separating control from unrestricted rights to extract profits or sell the enterprise.

The steward-ownership principles connect decision-making to people responsible for the organization and direct economic value toward its purpose. Different structures implement those commitments differently; the term names a design approach rather than one standard legal form.

sections.title: Protecting purpose, choosing stewards
sections.html:
Imagine a specialist publishing company whose stewards want to keep important but modest-selling books available. Restrictions on sale and profit extraction could protect that commitment from an owner seeking a quick exit. They would not determine which books deserve support or how to run the company well.

Those judgments still depend on people. A durable mission can become an excuse for unaccountable insiders if nobody can challenge or replace ineffective stewards. Employees and customers also need not receive decision rights merely because conventional shareholders have been constrained.

Steward ownership makes the future sale or diversion of an enterprise harder in particular ways. Its accompanying governance must answer who may act in the purpose's name, how successors are chosen, and how the organization can adapt without making its stated purpose meaningless.

title: Revenue sharing
description: Revenue sharing divides incoming sales among participants under an agreed rule, linking payment to receipts rather than to a later calculation of profit.
opening_html:
A musician and a distribution platform can agree that each sale will be split between them. The platform earns more when sales increase, and the musician receives the agreed portion. Revenue sharing connects their returns to a common stream of transactions.

Bandcamp takes a share of sales, with the remainder going to artists or labels. The percentage is only meaningful alongside the definition of the revenue being divided and the treatment of other charges.

sections.title: The percentage needs a base
sections.html:
Imagine two organizers sharing ticket revenue from a small performance. One pays for the venue and the other contributes promotion. A half-and-half split of receipts does not produce equal net earnings when their expenses differ. That may be acceptable, but it is a different agreement from dividing what remains after costs.

Refunds, payment charges, and reporting also affect the result. Someone must record sales in a way the other party can inspect. Double-entry accounting is one way to structure the underlying records. Without that visibility, a clear-looking percentage can conceal an uncertain amount.

Revenue sharing can make collaboration possible when participants want ongoing participation in sales rather than a fixed payment upfront. It does not by itself share ownership or decision-making. The arrangement coordinates a particular flow of money; the rest of the relationship still needs its own terms.

title: Profit sharing
description: Profit sharing distributes part of an organization’s surplus to participants, linking a payment to the results left after defined costs.
opening_html:
A team works through a demanding year and the business earns a surplus. Profit sharing gives employees or other participants an agreed portion of that result. It can recognize collective performance without allocating every sale to the person nearest the customer.

Unlike revenue sharing, the amount depends on what remains after costs. Buffer’s published arrangement ties a team bonus pool to net income rather than gross receipts.

sections.title: The surplus has to be defined
sections.html:
Imagine a design studio deciding whether to buy new equipment this year. The decision may affect reported profit and therefore the amount available for sharing. Participants need to understand the accounting basis and who controls decisions that change it.

The distribution rule matters too. Making the compensation formula transparent lets participants examine its criteria. Equal shares, hours worked, and other formulas express different views of contribution. A generous total can still create resentment if the division seems arbitrary or if people doing necessary support work are excluded.

Profit sharing can add a connection between the group's results and individual rewards. But workers usually cannot control every factor affecting the surplus, from lost customers to management choices. A bonus is therefore a particular financial arrangement, not a substitute for predictable pay or a voice in governance. The distinction keeps a promise of shared results from being mistaken for shared control.

title: Transparent compensation formulas
description: Transparent compensation formulas make the factors determining pay visible, allowing people to understand and challenge decisions that otherwise happen behind closed doors.
opening_html:
Two colleagues doing similar work discover very different salaries. The difference might reflect responsibilities, experience, negotiation history, or a manager's preference—but they cannot tell. A transparent compensation formula exposes the factors the organization says it uses to set pay.

The formula might connect a role and level to a benchmark, with other stated adjustments. A profit-sharing formula can likewise make the division of a bonus pool explicit. Buffer revised its salary formula when complexity and subjective decisions undermined its intended consistency. Publishing a formula leaves the organization responsible for choosing its inputs.

sections.title: Fairness moves into the inputs
sections.html:
Imagine a small organization publishing salary bands but assigning people to levels privately. Much of the consequential judgment remains hidden inside that assignment. Making the arithmetic visible helps, yet people also need to understand how their work maps to the inputs.

A location adjustment raises a different question: should identical work receive different pay because employees live in different places? A formula can apply either choice consistently without settling which choice the organization ought to make.

The useful change is that compensation becomes discussable in shared terms. People can identify an inconsistency or dispute a principle rather than merely wonder what a colleague negotiated. Updating the formula then becomes an explicit institutional decision, with consequences for people whose circumstances fit its categories imperfectly.
