title: Intellectual property
description: Assign rights over inventions, creative expression, and other intangible assets, shaping who may use them and on what terms.
opening_html:
If you lend someone a chair, you temporarily lose its use. If you show them a design, you can both retain the information. Creating that design may take months even when making another copy takes seconds. Intellectual property organizes rights around this difference.

The family includes several distinct arrangements. Patents concern qualifying inventions; copyright concerns original expression; trade secrets concern valuable confidential information. Trademarks serve another purpose: distinguishing the source of goods or services. These are not interchangeable ways of owning every idea.

sections.title: Permission and payment are separate choices
sections.html:
Imagine a designer publishing an illustrated manual for a new repair device. Rights in the text and drawings do not automatically provide rights over the device’s working principle. Someone seeking to reproduce the manual and someone seeking to manufacture a device are asking different questions.

Rights can create bargaining power, but they do not supply customers or finance development by themselves. Open licensing uses rights to grant permissions in advance; grants can pay for work without depending on later permission fees. Public access and compensation depend on how these arrangements are combined.

The interesting design choices concern what is protected, for how long, with which exceptions, and who can enforce the rights. Expanding control may make one investment easier to recover while making later learning and invention more expensive. The label alone does not settle that balance.

sections.title: An invention can earn money without exclusive control
sections.html:
A workshop may publish a pump design while customers still pay its team to manufacture reliably, install the equipment, and maintain it. The advantage lies in complementary capabilities rather than permission to copy. A survey of US manufacturing firms reported manufacturing and marketing capabilities among the ways firms captured returns from invention; that does not establish the same route for every industry.

The social arrangements around those capabilities still matter. Contracts organize paid production or support, licenses set reuse permissions, and partnerships can connect an inventor to a producer. A subscription may fund genuinely continuing service. None follows automatically from publishing a design.

This route is weaker when rivals can reproduce the whole offering cheaply. It may also reward the distributor more than the inventor. The relevant question is who controls the capabilities that customers need, and what agreement lets the people doing the inventive work share in the returns.

title: Patents
description: Offer time-limited exclusion rights over qualifying inventions in exchange for disclosure, creating one possible route to recovering development costs.
opening_html:
Imagine spending years developing a pump that uses less energy. Once it works, another manufacturer may be able to reproduce it much more cheaply than you could invent it. A patent changes that situation by giving its holder a legal basis to exclude specified uses of the protected invention.

A patent combines time-limited rights with public disclosure. Protection depends on the claims, territory, and applicable rules. It is an exclusion right, not a guarantee that the product is useful, profitable, or permitted to be sold under every other rule.

The holder might manufacture the pump or license others to do so. That opportunity can help attract investment. Yet obtaining and enforcing rights costs money, customers may prefer another design, and overlapping rights can complicate further development.

sections.title: Other ways to pay for discovery
sections.html:
The goal of rewarding invention does not require every payment to come from restricting its use. Commissioned research and development and grants can fund the attempt. Prize competitions reward a defined achievement. Advance market commitments make demand for a qualifying product more credible. These arrangements differ in who bears the risk and when money arrives.

A patent buyout can compensate a holder and release rights for wider use. Alternatively, trade secrets retain an advantage through confidentiality, while complementary capabilities can earn revenue from production, installation, or service even when the idea is available to others.

Each route has a different bottleneck: defining success, financing unsuccessful attempts, maintaining a secret, valuing rights, or delivering something customers continue to need. Copyright does a different job again: protecting a description of the pump would not, by itself, protect its working principle.

title: Copyright
description: Give creators and other rightsholders control over specified uses of original expression, while leaving underlying ideas outside that protection.
opening_html:
An illustrator may spend months making a field guide that another publisher could reproduce quickly. Copyright gives rights over specified uses of that work, making permission something the rightsholder can grant, withhold, or license for payment.

The crucial boundary is that copyright protects expression rather than the underlying ideas or methods. The illustrations and wording of a guide are different from the facts it describes. Writing about a new machine does not by itself secure the kind of protection associated with patents.

Imagine the illustrator permitting a school to translate the guide. The agreement can specify what may be reproduced and adapted. With open licensing, permissions can instead be offered in advance to an open-ended public, reducing repeated negotiations.

sections.title: Rights can also organize sharing
sections.html:
Copyleft uses copyright-based conditions to preserve specified freedoms when covered work is redistributed. Sharing under such terms is an exercise of rights, not necessarily their abandonment.

The same rights can make reuse difficult when the holder is hard to find or permissions are fragmented. Scope, duration, exceptions, and ownership rules vary across legal systems. Having rights also does not ensure an income: readers must still want the work, or another arrangement such as patronage must support its creation. The social mechanism joins creative work to decisions about access, adaptation, and payment.

title: Trade secrets
description: Preserve an advantage through valuable confidential knowledge and arrangements that limit its unauthorized acquisition or disclosure.
opening_html:
A manufacturer may sell a familiar-looking product while using a production process that competitors cannot observe. Keeping that process confidential can preserve an advantage without publishing it in a patent application.

Trade-secret protection depends on valuable secret information and reasonable steps to protect it. Access controls, working practices, and confidentiality agreements help make secrecy an organizational arrangement rather than a wish that nobody talks.

The firm can earn from using the knowledge or negotiate its licensed disclosure. But a rival who independently develops the same process, or lawfully learns it through reverse engineering, is in a different position from someone who steals confidential information. Secrecy does not create an exclusive right against every independent inventor.

sections.title: What must remain hidden?
sections.html:
Imagine a device whose construction becomes clear as soon as someone dismantles it. Confidential documents at the original workshop may do little to preserve the advantage once the product is sold. A less visible production technique presents a different situation.

Keeping knowledge restricted can also make training, collaboration, and succession harder. Tacit knowledge and secrecy are distinct: knowledge can be hard to explain without being deliberately withheld. The choice concerns both how the inventor can earn and what others must be prevented from learning.

title: Advance market commitments
description: Make future demand more credible by committing funding toward purchases of products that meet specified requirements.
opening_html:
A useful product may never be developed because its prospective users cannot credibly promise a market large enough to repay the investment. An advance market commitment brings a buyer or funder into the picture before the product or supply capacity is ready.

The commitment ties funding to qualifying supply under stated terms. In the pneumococcal vaccine AMC, donor funds supported manufacturer supply commitments alongside requirements for affordable long-term provision. The purchase commitment concerned supply and affordability as well as the existence of a qualifying vaccine.

sections.title: A customer before the product
sections.html:
Imagine towns jointly committing to buy a low-maintenance water sensor if it meets an agreed performance and price threshold. Developers can now assess a more concrete prospect of revenue. The towns still need to define a useful test, maintain funding, and decide how qualifying suppliers share the opportunity.

A prize competition pays for selected achievement; an AMC connects payment to purchasing and supply. Commissioned R&D pays for development work itself. The distinction changes which risks remain with the inventor.

An AMC need not prohibit patents or pay inventors directly rather than manufacturers. Open access must be addressed in its terms if that is part of the purpose. Its distinctive contribution is reducing uncertainty about demand; technical failure, production costs, and competition can still prevent a return.

title: Commissioned research and development
description: Pay a team to investigate or develop a solution, assigning development risks, payments, and rights through an agreement.
opening_html:
A transport operator needs a component that lasts longer under heavy use. Waiting for someone to invent it independently may not solve the problem. The operator can commission a team to investigate designs, build prototypes, and test them.

The contract makes development itself something a customer buys. Payment might cover work, milestones, or agreed results. Public-sector pre-commercial procurement can compare competing solutions through staged development and testing.

sections.title: Paying for the attempt
sections.html:
Unlike a prize competition that pays selected winners after achievement, a commission can provide revenue while work proceeds. That makes it a possible route to recovering development costs without relying entirely on later patent licensing. It does not make uncertain research risk-free or guarantee a profit.

The agreement must address what happens when a technically responsible attempt fails and who may use the resulting knowledge. Intellectual property can remain with the supplier, be transferred, or be licensed under negotiated terms. Paying for development does not automatically give the public permission to reproduce the result.

A narrow specification can reward compliance with the wrong target; an open-ended brief can make progress hard to assess. The relationship works through continuing judgments about evidence, scope, and responsibility. The customer is helping carry the uncertainty of invention, not simply ordering a finished item from a catalog.

title: Patent buyouts
description: Compensate a patent holder for releasing rights so others can use an invention more freely.
opening_html:
A useful invention can exist while access remains costly or permission is difficult to obtain. A patent buyout offers a different bargain: compensate the holder now, then release the relevant rights for wider use.

The mechanism begins with patents rather than replacing the patent system at the outset. It separates the payment for an invention from a continuing requirement that every user pay the holder. A buyout must actually release or broadly license rights to achieve that purpose; an ordinary transfer to a new exclusive owner does not.

sections.title: What is the price of opening access?
sections.html:
One economic proposal uses auctions to estimate patent value, then offers a buyout at a markup. The proposal depends on eliciting useful bids while limiting opportunities to inflate them.

The buyer faces an information problem. Expected commercial income and wider social value can differ substantially. An offer that is too low may be refused; an inflated offer spends funds that could support other discoveries. Bids and valuations can also be manipulated.

Even successful acquisition of a patent may leave production know-how, equipment, or other rights missing. Wider legal permission is a beginning, not a factory. Compared with prizes or grants, a buyout addresses an invention whose rights already exist. Whether it encourages future investment depends partly on how credible future rewards appear.
